title: Asana Technology Partners Overview
snippet:
Asana Technology Partners is designed for developers, ISVs, and tech companies seeking to build integrated solutions on the Asana platform. The program is ideal for those who develop custom applications, enhance product offerings, and deliver streamlined workflows. It offers co-selling opportunities, early API access, and dedicated support. Partners benefit from structured training and business incentives, ensuring a clear path to scalable success.
## Program benefits & incentives
Join the Asana Technology Partners Program to unlock the full potential of the Asana platform. This program is designed for tech partners, developers, and API integrators. Key benefits include: - Access to up-to-date APIs and a dedicated developer portal - Co-marketing incentives and revenue share opportunities - Comprehensive support resources to accelerate integration - Structured onboarding and continuous training - Direct product insights to keep you ahead These incentives empower partners to innovate, streamline workflows, and achieve scalable growth.
## Resources
## FAQ
Asana offers several flexible partnership paths including Technology, Solutions, Services, and Referral Partner programs, each tailored to different business models and expertise.
Partners enjoy revenue incentives, co-selling opportunities, marketing support including MDF, access to a dedicated Partner Portal, training through the Partner Academy, and early access to API and product updates.
Applicants must have an active Asana subscription and complete the partner application. Eligibility criteria can vary by program, with some requiring role-based certifications or proven SaaS experience.
New partners receive onboarding support through the Partner Portal, including access to role-based training, regular webinars, and a dedicated support team to ensure a smooth transition.
There is no upfront cost to join. However, partners must maintain an active Asana subscription as part of the program requirements.

title: Authentication
snippet:
A [personal access token](/docs/personal-access-token) (PAT) is the quickest and simplest way to authenticate in the API. PATs are long-lived tokens allowing programmatic authentication to the API and should be stored securely. PATs provide the same authorization (i.e., permissions and level of access to Asana data) through the *API* as the user who generated them has in the Asana *web product*.

Similar to PATs, [Service Accounts](https://help.asana.com/s/article/service-accounts) (SAs) are long-lived tokens that provide programmatic access to the API. Service Accounts are an [Enterprise tier](https://asana.com/enterprise) feature and can only be created by Asana super admins (see more about [admin roles at Asana](https://help.asana.com/s/article/admin-and-super-admin-roles-in-asana)).
Unlike PATs, SAs provide complete access to all data within your Asana account, including private user data. As such, SAs are ideal if your app needs to have org-wide authorization. Some common use cases include:
- Creating periodic data backups
- Automating programmatic management of your Asana account. For example:
- User management and access based on company's policies
- Administrative tasks like team member management
- Cleaning up inactive projects
- Standardizing the structure of objects in your domain (e.g., portfolios, projects, custom fields, etc.)
- Building integrations that require access to all Asana data
- Authenticating Asana API endpoints that require service accounts. For example:
- [Audit log](/reference/audit-log-api)
- [Organizational exports](/reference/organization-exports)
- [SCIM](/docs/scim)

title: Asana API Guide: Get Tasks, Projects, and Users in 2026
snippet:
Asana's API is a REST interface that speaks JSON at `https://app.asana.com/api/1.0`, and you can list tasks with a personal access token and a `GET /tasks` call, the same kind of call that tools like [Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com) make under the hood when they talk to Asana.

### Which Asana plans include API access
You create a personal access token from your own account's developer settings, and Asana's developer documentation describes the API as available to Asana accounts.
Plan details change over time. Confirm them on Asana's pricing page and the developer docs before you build a dependency on a particular tier. To check access, make a single `GET /users/me` call with your token.

| | Personal access token | OAuth app | Service account |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who it acts as | The user who created it | Each user who authorizes the app | A dedicated non-human user, where your Asana plan offers one |
| Best for | Your own scripts and one-off pulls | Products used by other people | Unattended jobs that should outlive any one employee |
| How it's sent | `Authorization: Bearer <token>` | `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` | `Authorization: Bearer <token>` |
| Scopes behaviour | Carries the full access of its owner | Limited to the scopes the user approves | Limited to what that account can see |
| Setup effort | Minutes, from the developer console | Registration, redirect URI, consent flow, token refresh | Account provisioning, then a token like any other |

1. Create a personal access token in your Asana account settings, and store it as a secret rather than in the source.

title: OAuth
snippet:
At its core, OAuth ("Open Authorization") is a mechanism for applications to access the Asana API on behalf of a user, all without the application having access to the user's username and password. Instead, the application gets a *token*, which can be used in subsequent API calls through the addition of an [Authorization header](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Authorization):
```
-H "Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN"
```
